endorsements.quote: Participants consistently emphasised the importance of involving underserved and diverse communities, including patient representatives, throughout the entire AI lifecycle.

Assigning ownership of each element to a named role (e.g., a team member responsible for sustained Participatory and co-design engagement (P)) counters the diffusion of responsibility that often leaves inclusivity unattended.

Participants highlighted the need for targeted educational initiatives to enhance the understanding of AI among patients, HCP, and the broader public, addressing both the potential benefits and risks.

unlisted_practices: Establish a multi-stakeholder advisory panel on inclusive AI to be engaged throughout the development of regulatory frameworks.
Develop a compliance support tool and toolbox to help developers and institutions navigate ethical and regulatory requirements for inclusive AI.
Establish a European-level curriculum or training programme to build AI literacy and capacity of patient representatives.
Embed data literacy in healthcare education.
Create structural incentives, such as linking funding eligibility to data literacy and inclusivity actions.

Embed inclusivity requirements into existing governance checkpoints such as research ethics review, data protection impact assessments, clinical validation gates, and procurement and funding criteria.
Plan, resource, and budget patient participation from the proposal stage, with patient representatives helping define research questions and metrics.
Document when interoperable data standards cannot represent relevant determinants of health, record why the team proceeds, and specify a local adaptation mechanism.

screen.reason: Presents a co-created framework (PREFER-IT) offering guidelines and recommendations for inclusive health AI across design, deployment, and governance based on an expert workshop.
